a.wave-function-collapse.summary: A procedural generation algorithm that generates tilemaps and levels by fixing cells, lowest-entropy first, and propagating local pattern constraints taken from an example image.
a.wavefront-alignment.summary: A gap-affine pairwise alignment algorithm that, for each score s, computes only the furthest-reaching position on each diagonal (the wavefront) and slides along matching stretches. It takes O(ns) time for sequence length n and optimal score s, so it is fast on similar sequences.
a.wavelet-matrix.summary: A structure that concatenates the bit vectors of each wavelet-tree level into a single one without node boundaries and, at every level, stably moves elements with bit 0 to the front and those with bit 1 to the back. It answers the same queries as a wavelet tree with one bit vector per level and no tree pointers, even for large alphabets.
a.wavelet-tree.summary: A binary tree that recursively halves the alphabet of a string and stores at each node a bit vector telling which half each character belongs to. Using rank and select on the bit vectors, it supports access, rank and select for any symbol in O(log σ) time and underlies compressed text indexes.
a.wavenet.summary: A generative model of raw audio waveforms that stacks dilated causal convolutions to predict each sample autoregressively, conditioned on the previous samples. It was applied to text-to-speech.
a.wavl-tree.o0.note: The journal version appeared in ACM Transactions on Algorithms 11(4), 2015.
a.wavl-tree.summary: A balanced binary search tree that gives each node an integer rank and restricts every parent–child rank difference to 1 or 2. Without deletions it coincides with an AVL tree, and each insertion or deletion performs at most two rotations.
a.wegman-carter-mac.summary: A method that hashes a message with a strongly universal hash function and masks it with a one-time key to obtain information-theoretically secure authentication. It became the template for modern MACs such as Poly1305, GCM and UMAC.
a.weight-balanced-tree.o0.note: The journal version appeared in SIAM Journal on Computing 2(1), 1973.
a.weight-balanced-tree.summary: A binary search tree that uses rotations to keep the ratio of left and right subtree sizes at every node within a fixed bound α. Because subtree sizes are stored, it also supports rank queries.
a.weight-norm.summary: A reparameterization that splits each weight vector into a direction vector and a scalar magnitude that are learned separately. It speeds up optimization without relying on minibatch statistics.
a.weighted-fair-queuing.summary: Scheduling that assigns a weight to each flow and transmits packets in the order in which they would finish under the fluid Generalized Processor Sharing (GPS) model. It guarantees delay bounds for flows constrained by leaky buckets.
a.weighted-reservoir-sampling.summary: Assigns each item of weight w the key u^(1/w), where u is a uniform random number, and keeps the k items with the largest keys, drawing a weighted random sample from a stream in one pass.
a.weighted-voting.summary: A replicated-data management technique that assigns votes to each copy and chooses a read quorum r and write quorum w with r + w greater than the total number of votes, so that every read overlaps the latest write.
a.weiler-atherton.summary: Clipping algorithm that inserts the intersection points of two polygons into both boundary lists and then builds the result by starting at an entering intersection and alternately following the two boundaries. Concave polygons and polygons with holes can serve as clip regions; it was originally proposed for hidden surface removal.
a.well-rng.summary: A family of long-period pseudorandom generators based on linear recurrences over GF(2). By mixing state bits more thoroughly, it improves equidistribution and recovery from states with many zero bits compared with the Mersenne Twister.
a.welsh-powell.summary: A greedy graph-colouring method that sorts vertices by decreasing degree and gives each, in turn, the smallest available colour. An upper bound on the chromatic number obtained from this order was presented with it.
a.welzl.summary: Randomized algorithm that adds points in random order and, whenever a point falls outside the current smallest enclosing circle, recomputes it recursively with that point fixed on the boundary, finding the minimum enclosing circle in expected linear time. It generalizes to smallest enclosing balls and ellipsoids in higher dimensions.
a.whitted-ray-tracing.summary: A ray tracing method that recursively traces reflection, refraction, and shadow rays from each intersection point.
a.wichmann-hill.summary: A generator that produces uniform variates by scaling the outputs of three multiplicative congruential generators with different moduli to [0, 1), adding them and taking the fractional part. Its period is about 6.95×10¹².
a.williams-p-plus-1.summary: A factorization algorithm that uses Lucas sequences to find a prime factor p when p+1 has only small prime factors. It is the counterpart of Pollard's p−1 method.
a.winnowing.summary: A document fingerprinting algorithm that selects as fingerprints the minimum hash in each window of size w over the sequence of k-gram hashes of a document. It guarantees that any match above a certain length is detected and is used in plagiarism detection.
a.winograd-fft.summary: A DFT algorithm that computes short-length DFTs as convolutions with a near-minimal number of multiplications and combines them via prime-factor index mapping, reducing the total multiplication count.
a.wireguard.summary: A kernel-level VPN tunnel protocol that fixes Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and BLAKE2s on top of the Noise Protocol Framework's IK handshake. Its code base is small, its configuration simple, and it is included in the Linux kernel.
a.wolff-algorithm.summary: A single-cluster Monte Carlo method that grows one cluster from a randomly chosen seed spin by probabilistically adding aligned neighbors and then flips that cluster. Using reflections, it also applies to continuous spin systems such as O(n) models.
a.word2vec.summary: A method that learns word vectors by training shallow models on large corpora to predict a center word from its context (CBOW) or the context from a center word (skip-gram).
a.wordpiece.summary: A subword tokenization method that builds a vocabulary of word pieces by repeatedly adding the unit that most increases language-model likelihood. It was devised for Japanese and Korean voice search and is used in BERT.
a.work-stealing.o0.note: The journal version appeared in J. ACM 46(5), 1999 (doi:10.1145/324133.324234).
a.work-stealing.summary: A multithreaded scheduling algorithm in which each processor takes work from one end of its own deque and, when idle, steals work from the other end of a randomly chosen processor's deque. Provable bounds on execution time and space are known.
a.working-set-model.summary: A memory-management model that defines a process's working set as the pages it referenced during a recent time window and controls page allocation and the degree of multiprogramming so that working sets stay resident. It is used to prevent thrashing.
a.worley-noise.summary: A procedural texture basis function that uses the distance to the n-th nearest of feature points randomly scattered in space. It produces patterns with Voronoi-like structure such as cells, stones and scales.
a.wound-wait.summary: A preemptive deadlock-prevention scheme that gives transactions start timestamps; on a lock conflict an older transaction aborts (wounds) the younger lock holder, while a younger requester waits.
a.wu-manber-agrep.summary: An approximate string search algorithm that keeps one Shift-Or bit vector per allowed number of errors, permitting up to k insertions, deletions and substitutions. It is one of the core algorithms implemented in the approximate search tool agrep.
a.wu-manber.summary: A multi-pattern search algorithm that skips text windows using a shift table indexed by hashed character blocks of length B and directly compares only the candidate patterns whose hash matches. It remains fast on average even with many patterns.
a.x-fast-trie.summary: A binary trie over integer keys that stores the prefixes of each level in hash tables and links the leaves in a list. It answers predecessor and successor queries in O(log log u) time using O(n log u) space.
a.x25519.summary: A Diffie–Hellman key exchange that computes scalar multiplication using only x-coordinates on the Montgomery curve Curve25519. It is fast and easy to implement in constant time, and is widely used in TLS 1.3, SSH, Signal and WireGuard.
a.x3dh.summary: A key-agreement protocol that establishes a shared secret asynchronously, even while the peer is offline, by combining several Diffie–Hellman computations over identity keys, signed prekeys and one-time prekeys. It was used to start sessions in the Signal Protocol.
a.xavier-init.summary: A weight initialization that sets the variance to 2/(n_in + n_out) from a layer's fan-in and fan-out. It aims to keep the variance of activations and back-propagated gradients stable across layers.
a.xex-mode.summary: A construction that turns a block cipher into a tweakable block cipher by XORing a tweak-derived mask before and after encryption. It underlies the XTS disk-encryption mode.
a.xgboost.summary: Scalable gradient boosting that adds a second-order approximation of the objective, regularization, sparsity-aware split finding, and cache optimization.
a.xiaolin-wu-line.summary: An antialiased line algorithm that divides intensity, in proportion to distance, between the two pixels the line straddles.
a.xmss.summary: A stateful hash-based signature that improves the Merkle signature scheme, proving security under minimal assumptions (a second-preimage-resistant hash and a PRF) and providing forward security. It is standardized in RFC 8391 and NIST SP 800-208.
a.xor-filter.summary: A static approximate membership filter whose table is built so that each key's fingerprint equals the XOR of the three slots the key maps to. It aims to be smaller and faster than Bloom and cuckoo filters.
a.xorshift.summary: A family of very fast pseudorandom number generators that update their state using only shifts and XORs.
a.xoshiro.summary: A family of pseudorandom number generators that improves on xorshift's statistical quality by adding rotations and an output scrambler.
a.xpbd.summary: An extension of position-based dynamics that introduces per-constraint compliance (inverse stiffness) and accumulated Lagrange multipliers so that stiffness no longer depends on the iteration count and time step. It allows specifying physical stiffness corresponding to elastic potentials.
a.xts.summary: A mode of operation for encrypting fixed-size storage units such as disk sectors. It adds ciphertext stealing to the XEX construction, uses the sector number as the tweak, and is used by BitLocker, FileVault and dm-crypt.
a.xxhash.summary: A family of non-cryptographic hash functions designed to run close to memory bandwidth. It consists of the 32-bit XXH32, the 64-bit XXH64 and the vectorized XXH3.
a.y-fast-trie.summary: A structure that partitions the keys into groups of size O(log u), keeps each group in a balanced binary search tree, and stores only one representative per group in an x-fast trie. It answers predecessor and successor queries in O(log log u) time with O(n) space.
a.yao-garbled-circuits.o0.note: The garbled-circuit technique is generally attributed to the oral presentation of this work, and its concrete form was written down in later papers.
a.yao-garbled-circuits.summary: A two-party secure computation technique in which one party garbles each gate of a Boolean circuit into an encrypted truth table and the other evaluates the circuit holding only the keys for its own inputs. It lets the parties compute any function without revealing their inputs to each other.
a.yarrow.summary: A cryptographic pseudorandom number generator composed of entropy accumulators, a reseed mechanism and a block-cipher-based output generator. It reseeds from fast and slow pools according to entropy estimates and was used in /dev/random on macOS and FreeBSD.
a.yen-k-shortest-paths.summary: An algorithm that finds the k shortest loopless paths one by one: for each vertex of the previously found path, it fixes the prefix up to that vertex, blocks edges that would repeat already found paths, and computes the shortest remaining spur path.
a.yolo.summary: A real-time object detector in which a single convolutional network divides the image into a grid and regresses bounding boxes and class probabilities in one forward pass.
a.yuasa-snapshot-barrier.summary: A write-barrier technique for incremental and concurrent marking that marks the object a pointer previously referred to before the pointer is overwritten, so that every object reachable when marking began survives.
a.z-buffer.summary: A hidden-surface removal technique that stores the nearest depth value for each pixel to eliminate occluded surfaces pixel by pixel.
a.z-order-curve.summary: Method that orders multidimensional points along one dimension by the value obtained by interleaving the binary digits of their coordinates. Since it needs only bit operations, it is used in spatial indexes, memory layouts and geohash, among others.
a.zab.summary: A primary-backup atomic broadcast protocol in which a leader proposes state changes in order and commits them after acknowledgment by a majority, and on leader change recovers prior history using epochs and a synchronization phase. It is used in Apache ZooKeeper.
a.zhang-calibration.summary: Camera calibration that computes a homography for each image of a planar pattern (such as a checkerboard) viewed from several orientations, initializes the intrinsic and extrinsic parameters with a closed-form solution, and refines them by maximum-likelihood estimation.
a.zhang-suen-thinning.summary: A parallel thinning algorithm that alternately deletes boundary pixels that do not break connectivity in two subiterations, producing a one-pixel-wide skeleton of a binary image.
a.ziggurat.o0.note: The simplified form in wide use today appeared in the same authors' 2000 Journal of Statistical Software paper 'The Ziggurat Method for Generating Random Variables'.
a.ziggurat.summary: A rejection sampling method that precomputes a table of equal-area horizontal strips covering the region under a decreasing density, so most samples need only a table lookup and one comparison. It is widely used to generate normal and exponential variates.
a.zip-tree.o0.note: Later published at WADS 2019 and in ACM Transactions on Algorithms (2021).
a.zip-tree.summary: A randomized binary search tree that gives each node a rank drawn from a geometric distribution and keeps the tree heap-ordered by rank. Insertions and deletions use unzip and zip operations on paths instead of rotations, and the tree is equivalent to a tree representation of a skip list.
a.zipper.summary: A representation technique for immutable data structures such as trees that stores the current position (focus) together with the context of the path leading to it. Moving around and editing near the focus take constant time.
a.zobrist-hashing.summary: Builds a position hash by assigning a random bit string to each (square, piece) combination and XOR-ing those present on the board. The hash is updated incrementally by XOR-ing only the changed entries when a move is made or undone, and is used for transposition tables.
a.zopfli.o0.note: According to the repository README, it was created by Lode Vandevenne and Jyrki Alakuijala and is based on an algorithm by Jyrki Alakuijala.
a.zopfli.summary: A DEFLATE-compatible compressor that optimizes LZ77 parsing by iterating entropy-model estimation and shortest-path search. Compression is slow, but it produces smaller output that existing zlib and gzip decompressors can decode.
a.zstd.summary: A compression method that encodes LZ77 matches with tANS (FSE) and Huffman codes. It offers a wide range of speeds and compression ratios.
e.a-star>alt: The report proposes shortest-path algorithms that combine A* search with a lower-bounding technique based on landmarks and the triangle inequality.
e.a-star>d-star: Named as a dynamic A* for environments with changing costs
e.a-star>ida-star: Presented as iterative deepening on A*'s f-value bound
e.a-star>jump-point-search: Presented as pruning that reduces the nodes A* expands to jump points
e.a-star>lpa-star: The paper presents LPA* as an incremental version of A* that uses heuristics.
e.a-star>theta-star: The paper presents Theta* as a variant of A* that propagates information along grid edges.
e.abp-deque>chase-lev-deque: Chase and Lev presented a circular-array deque that removes the fixed-size array limitation of the ABP deque
e.actor-critic>a3c: A3C is a variant that trains an advantage actor-critic asynchronously across multiple threads.
e.actor-critic>ddpg: DDPG is presented as a model-free actor-critic algorithm based on the deterministic policy gradient.
e.actor-critic>sac: SAC is presented as an off-policy actor-critic algorithm with a maximum-entropy objective.
e.actor-critic>td-lambda: Sutton's TD paper treats the adaptive critic element of Barto et al. as an earlier instance of temporal-difference methods.
e.adaboost>gradient-boosting: Interprets AdaBoost as a stagewise additive model and generalizes it to arbitrary losses
e.adaboost>viola-jones: The Viola–Jones paper states that it uses AdaBoost to select a small number of Haar-like features and train each stage classifier
e.adagrad>adam: The Adam paper states that it combines the advantages of AdaGrad and RMSProp
e.adagrad>rmsprop: Replaces AdaGrad's accumulated sum of squares with a moving average (Adam paper, related work section)
e.adam>adafactor: Adafactor modifies Adam by factoring its second-moment estimate to save memory
e.adam>adamw: Presents a modification of Adam with decoupled weight decay
e.adam>lamb: LAMB is defined by multiplying Adam's update by a layer-wise trust ratio
e.adamw>lion: The program search that discovered Lion was initialized with AdamW
e.adaptive-huffman>vitter-algorithm: Vitter's paper analyzes the FGK algorithm and presents a dynamic Huffman algorithm with a smaller bound on code length
e.additive-attention>dot-product-attenti: Proposes a simpler scoring function, compared against Bahdanau attention
e.additive-attention>gat: The GAT paper draws on the attention work of Bahdanau et al. and applies attention over graph neighborhoods
e.aes>aria: Uses an SPN structure like AES with two kinds of S-boxes, one of which is the AES S-box
e.aho-corasick>commentz-walter: Described as combining an Aho–Corasick-style trie of the (reversed) patterns with Boyer–Moore-style skipping.
e.aimd>tcp-slow-start: TCP congestion avoidance applies the additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease rule, and both works appeared in the same period.
e.alexnet>r-cnn: R-CNN extracts region features with the convolutional network of Krizhevsky et al.
e.alexnet>vgg: Increases depth, taking the configuration of Krizhevsky et al. as the baseline
e.alias-method>vose-alias: Vose presents an algorithm that performs the table-construction step of Walker's alias method in linear time
e.aloha>binary-exponential-backoff: Metcalfe and Boggs state that the Ethernet design started from the collision-and-retransmission idea of the ALOHA network, and extended it by widening the retransmission interval on each collision.
e.aloha>slotted-aloha: Roberts analyzed the variant that introduces time slots into the ALOHA channel.
e.alpha-beta>history-heuristic: The paper presents the history heuristic as a technique for improving move ordering in alpha–beta search
e.alpha-beta>mtd-f: The paper formulates MTD(f) as repeated calls to a null-window alpha–beta search with memory
e.alpha-beta>principal-variation-search: References describe PVS/NegaScout as an improvement of alpha–beta that reduces search effort with null-window tests
e.alt-godau-frechet>discrete-frechet: The discrete Fréchet distance is a variant of the continuous Fréchet distance restricted to couplings of vertices, computed with a dynamic-programming table instead of the free-space diagram.
e.ans>zstd: The FSE of RFC 8878 is a tANS implementation
e.apriori>fp-growth: FP-growth was presented as a frequent-pattern mining method that avoids the costly candidate generation of Apriori-like methods.
e.arithmetic-coding>ans: Duda presented it as achieving both the compression ratio of arithmetic coding and the speed of Huffman coding
e.arithmetic-coding>cabac: As its title states, it is a context-based adaptive binary arithmetic coding scheme
e.arithmetic-coding>calic: CALIC codes its prediction residuals with context-based arithmetic coding
e.arithmetic-coding>ctw: The probabilities computed by CTW are coded with arithmetic coding
e.arithmetic-coding>dmc: DMC codes the probabilities of its bit-level Markov model with arithmetic coding
e.arithmetic-coding>ppm: As its title states, it combines adaptive (arithmetic) coding with a partial string matching model
e.arithmetic-coding>q-coder: As its title states, it is an adaptive binary arithmetic coder
e.arithmetic-coding>range-coding: Equivalent scheme that implements arithmetic coding with integer ranges and byte-wise output
e.arnoldi-iteration>gmres: The GMRES paper minimizes the residual over the basis built by the Arnoldi process.
e.arnoldi-iteration>implicitly-restarted: Sorensen's paper presents a restart technique that implicitly applies polynomial filters to the k-step Arnoldi method.
e.augmented-lagrangian>admm: ADMM is described as the augmented Lagrangian method with alternating minimization over blocks of variables.
e.avl-tree>wavl-tree: The paper relaxes the AVL condition so that a WAVL tree coincides with an AVL tree when there are no deletions.
e.b-link-tree>bw-tree: The Bw-tree paper keeps sibling links, as in B-link trees, so searches can proceed during splits.
e.b-tree>b-epsilon-tree: The paper shows the insertion–query trade-off using B-trees whose nodes carry buffers.
e.b-tree>b-link-tree: Lehman and Yao added a right link and a high key to B-tree nodes to allow concurrent access.
e.b-tree>birch: BIRCH's CF tree is designed as a height-balanced tree similar to a B+-tree.
e.b-tree>buffer-tree: The buffer tree is an (a,b)-tree, a member of the B-tree family, with a buffer attached to each internal node.
e.b-tree>finger-tree: The 2-3 finger tree places fingers at both ends of a 2-3 tree structure built from nodes of degree two or three.
e.b-tree>fusion-tree: A fusion tree is a B-tree whose node degree is a power of the word length, with comparisons inside a node done by word operations.
e.b-tree>gist: The GiST paper implements the B+-tree as one instance of the generalized search tree.
e.b-tree>kdb-tree: Like a B-tree, the K-D-B-tree is a balanced paged tree with all leaves at the same depth.
e.b-tree>lsm-tree: The LSM paper compares write costs with B-trees, but there is no derivation relationship
e.b-tree>masstree: Each layer of Masstree is a B+-tree indexing a slice of the key.
e.b-tree>r-tree: Describes the R-tree as a height-balanced tree similar to the B-tree
e.b-tree>sbb-tree: Bayer presented it as a binary-tree representation of B-trees
e.baby-step-giant-step>pohlig-hellman: Pohlig–Hellman reduces the problem to discrete logarithms in prime-order subgroups, and each subproblem is commonly solved with baby-step giant-step
e.baby-step-giant-step>pollard-rho-log: Both are generic O(√n)-time discrete logarithm algorithms; the rho method works without a table in constant memory
e.backpropagation>elman-network: The Elman network treats context units as extra inputs and is trained with backpropagation
e.backpropagation>lenet: As the paper's title says, applies backpropagation to training a convolutional neural network
e.bagging>random-forest: States that it combines bagging with random feature selection
e.baker-gc>brooks-forwarding-pointer: Brooks replaced the read barrier of Baker's collector with an indirection through a forwarding pointer in every object, reducing time and code size
e.batch-norm>group-norm: Group normalization is proposed as an alternative to batch normalization, which degrades with small batches
e.batch-norm>instance-norm: The paper proposes replacing batch normalization in style-transfer generators with instance normalization
e.batch-norm>layer-norm: Presented as batch normalization moved from the batch dimension to the layer dimension
e.batch-norm>resnet: States that batch normalization is applied after each convolution
e.batch-norm>weight-norm: Weight normalization was inspired by batch normalization and aims at a similar effect without depending on the minibatch
e.baum-welch>em: Dempster et al. cite the HMM estimation of Baum et al. as an instance of EM
e.bch-code>berlekamp-massey: As the title of Massey's paper says, the algorithm was presented for BCH decoding.
e.bch-code>chien-search: Chien's paper presents the error-location search as a cyclic decoding procedure for BCH codes.
e.bch-code>forney-algorithm: Forney's paper treats the computation of error values in decoding BCH codes.
e.bch-code>pgz-decoder: Peterson's paper gives error-correction procedures specifically for the Bose-Chaudhuri codes.
e.bch-code>reed-solomon: Reed–Solomon codes are now classified as a kind of non-binary BCH code, although they were published independently.
e.bcjr>turbo-code: Iterative turbo decoding uses component decoders based on a modified BCJR (MAP) algorithm.
e.bdf>lsoda: LSODA automatically selects BDF for stiff phases and Adams methods for nonstiff phases.
e.belief-propagation>affinity-propagatio: The message updates of affinity propagation are derived from max-sum belief propagation on a factor graph.
e.bellman-ford>cycle-canceling: Bellman–Ford-style negative-cycle detection is commonly used to find negative-cost cycles in the residual graph.
e.bellman-ford>delta-stepping: With large Δ it approaches the Bellman–Ford approach of repeatedly relaxing all edges.
e.bellman-ford>duan-sssp: Its pivot-finding step, which reduces the number of frontier vertices, runs a few rounds of Bellman–Ford-style relaxation.
e.bellman-ford>goldberg-radzik: As its title states, it is a heuristic improvement of the Bellman–Ford algorithm.
e.bellman-ford>johnson: Computes potentials with Bellman–Ford to reweight edges
e.bellman-ford>karp-min-mean-cycle: It computes shortest walks with k edges using the same recurrence as Bellman–Ford.
e.bellman-ford>raptor: Its structure of relaxing arrival times by scanning each route once per round resembles the round-based relaxation of Bellman–Ford.
e.bellman-ford>rip: RFC 1058 states that RIP is based on the Bellman-Ford (distance vector) algorithm.
e.bellman-ford>spfa: Queue-based improvement of Bellman–Ford that re-relaxes only updated vertices (the same idea appears in Moore 1959)
e.bender-farach-colton-lca>fischer-heun-: Fischer and Heun removed the ±1 restriction and the detour through LCA in the Bender–Farach-Colton method, handling RMQ directly.
e.bentley-mcilroy-partitioning>multikey-: The paper cites and uses the ternary partition of Bentley and McIlroy and notes that its complete code is similar to theirs.
e.bentley-ottmann>fortune: Applies the same plane-sweep technique to a different problem
e.bentley-ottmann>martinez-rueda: The Martínez–Rueda algorithm uses, for Boolean operations, the plane-sweep structure that processes edges in endpoint-event order and tests neighbouring edges for intersections.
e.berlekamp-factorization>cantor-zassenh: Cantor and Zassenhaus present a new algorithm for the same problem as Berlekamp's, factoring polynomials over finite fields, using random gcd splitting instead of linear algebra
e.bert>roberta: RoBERTa replicates BERT pretraining and tunes its design choices and training setup
e.bezier-curve>de-boor-algorithm: De Boor's algorithm generalizes de Casteljau's algorithm for Bézier curves to B-splines.
e.bfgs>l-bfgs: As its title states, the paper applies a limited-memory form of the BFGS method to large-scale optimization.
e.bfs>brandes-betweenness: On unweighted graphs it counts shortest paths with a breadth-first search from each source.
e.bfs>dijkstra: With all weights equal it visits vertices in the same order as BFS, but no evidence that it originated from BFS
e.bfs>edmonds-karp: Finds shortest augmenting paths with BFS (CLRS §26.2)
e.bfs>hopcroft-karp: Each phase uses BFS to build the layered graph of shortest augmenting paths.
e.bfs>lex-bfs: It is a search that replaces the next-vertex rule of breadth-first search with a comparison of lexicographic labels.
e.bgv>bfv: Manages noise with a scale-invariant technique instead of BGV's modulus switching
e.bic-tcp>cubic: The CUBIC paper presents CUBIC as an enhanced version of BIC that replaces its window growth with a cubic function.
e.bidirectional-path-tracing>metropolis-: MLT's bidirectional mutation deletes a subpath and regenerates it in the manner of bidirectional path tracing
e.bidirectional-rnn>ctc: The CTC experiments use a bidirectional recurrent architecture so that each frame sees both past and future context
e.bidirectional-search>contraction-hiera: Queries are answered with a bidirectional Dijkstra search that only follows upward edges.
e.bidirectional-search>highway-hierarchi: It answers queries with bidirectional search on the highway hierarchy built in preprocessing.
e.bilateral-filter>guided-filter: The guided filter is presented as an alternative that performs edge-preserving smoothing like the bilateral filter in linear time independent of kernel size
e.bilateral-filter>non-local-means: Non-local means extends neighborhood filters such as the bilateral filter by weighting with patch similarity instead of single-pixel similarity
e.binary-heap>binomial-heap: Generalizes heap-ordered trees to a forest as a mergeable priority queue
e.binary-heap>calendar-queue: The calendar queue solves the same priority-queue problem as the binary heap with a bucket array, without evidence of direct derivation.
e.binary-heap>d-ary-heap: The d-ary heap generalizes the number of children in a binary heap from two to d.
e.binary-heap>heapsort: Williams's Algorithm 232 defines the heap data structure and presents a sort that uses it
e.binary-heap>leftist-heap: The leftist heap keeps the same heap order as the binary heap but uses a pointer-based tree instead of an array to make merging fast.
e.binary-heap>min-max-heap: The min-max heap keeps the array representation of the binary heap while alternating min and max order between levels.
e.binary-heap>priority-search-tree: McCreight presented the priority search tree as a structure that combines the properties of a heap and a binary search tree.
e.binary-heap>treap: By definition, priorities satisfy heap order
e.binary-insertion-sort>merge-insertion: Structurally it binary-inserts the remaining elements, in a fixed order, into a main chain built from pairwise comparisons.
e.binary-insertion-sort>timsort: listsort.txt describes extending short runs to the minimum length with binary insertion sort
e.binary-search>exponential-search: The Bentley–Yao algorithm finds an upper bound exponentially, then performs binary search
e.binary-search>fibonacci-search: Like binary search it shrinks an interval of a sorted array, but chooses split points by Fibonacci numbers.
e.binary-search>fractional-cascading: Fractional cascading reduces repeated binary searches over many lists to one binary search plus constant-time steps.
e.binary-search>interpolation-search: Chooses the probe position by interpolating key values instead of taking the midpoint (treated together in Knuth TAOCP Vol.3 §6.2.1)
e.binary-search>jump-search: Both search sorted arrays, but jump search uses fixed-step jumps followed by a sequential scan.
e.binomial-heap>fibonacci-heap: Defines Fibonacci heaps as binomial queues with lazily deferred operations
e.binomial-heap>pairing-heap: Self-adjusting heap that simplifies binomial-heap merging to pairing within a single tree
e.binomial-heap>soft-heap: Chazelle describes the soft heap as built on binomial queues, modified to allow key corruption.
e.bitonic-sort>odd-even-merge-sort: Sorting networks presented together in the same paper; neither derives from the other
e.blake2>argon2: RFC 9106 uses BLAKE2b as Argon2's hash function
e.blake2>blake3: The BLAKE3 specification states that it reuses the BLAKE2s compression function with reduced rounds
e.blake2>wireguard: The paper states that BLAKE2s is used for hashing and key derivation
e.blake>blake2: Presented as an improvement of BLAKE with fewer rounds and an added parameter block
e.blast>blat: The tool's very name declares it a BLAST-like alignment tool, and it changes the indexing scheme for genome scale.
e.blockquicksort>pdqsort: The pdqsort source states that its branchless partitioning is derived from BlockQuicksort by Edelkamp and Weiss.
e.bloom-filter>blocked-bloom-filter: The paper presents a Bloom filter variant that groups an element's bits into one cache block to improve cache efficiency.
e.bloom-filter>count-min-sketch: Similar structure of marking array cells with multiple hashes, but no evidence of derivation
e.bloom-filter>counting-bloom-filter: Fan et al. extend Bloom filter bits to counters to support deletion
e.bloom-filter>cuckoo-filter: Compared as a replacement for Bloom filters, but not derived from them
e.bloom-filter>quotient-filter: An alternative structure for the same approximate membership problem that the Bloom filter solves.
e.bloom-filter>xor-filter: Addresses the same approximate membership problem; the paper compares it against Bloom filters and reports it as smaller and faster.
e.blowfish>bcrypt: Defines Eksblowfish, which repeats the Blowfish key schedule according to a cost factor
e.blowfish>twofish: A Feistel structure with key-dependent S-boxes, like Blowfish by the same designer
e.boids>steering-behaviors: Reynolds extended the flocking rules of boids into general steering behaviors for autonomous characters
e.boltzmann-machine>contrastive-divergen: Contrastive divergence approximates Boltzmann machine learning by replacing equilibrium sampling with a short Markov chain
e.booth-rotation>duval-lyndon: Least rotation and Lyndon factorization deal with the same lexicographic minimality, and Duval's algorithm can also compute least rotations.
e.boruvka>kruskal: Addresses the same minimum spanning tree problem, but no evidence of derivation
e.boruvka>prim: Jarník's 1930 manuscript was a letter to Borůvka solving the same problem in a different way
e.bose-nelson>odd-even-merge-sort: It is an earlier recursive construction for the same sorting-network problem.
e.boundary-package-merge>zopfli: Zopfli's katajainen.c states that it computes code lengths with the boundary package-merge algorithm based on the paper by Katajainen, Moffat and Turpin
e.box-muller>marsaglia-polar: The polar method is described as a variant of the Box–Muller transform that replaces the trigonometric evaluations with rejection sampling in the unit circle
e.boyer-moore>apostolico-giancarlo: The paper's title states that it revisits the Boyer–Moore–Galil search strategies, and it presents a variant of them.
e.boyer-moore>commentz-walter: Described as a generalization of the Boyer–Moore shift rules to searching for several patterns at once.
e.boyer-moore>galil-rule: Presented, as its title says, as a rule improving the worst-case running time of Boyer–Moore string matching.
e.boyer-moore>horspool: Presented as a simplification that keeps only Boyer–Moore's bad-character rule
e.boyer-moore>quick-search: Presented as a simplified variant that bases the Boyer–Moore bad-character shift on the character after the window.
e.boyer-moore>two-way-string-matching: The authors describe the algorithm as intermediate between Knuth–Morris–Pratt and Boyer–Moore.
e.bpe-tokenization>gpt: GPT uses a BPE vocabulary with 40,000 merges, citing Sennrich et al.
e.bpe-tokenization>sentencepiece: SentencePiece provides an implementation that trains BPE subword segmentation directly from raw text
e.brandes-betweenness>girvan-newman: Its repeated edge-betweenness computation corresponds to Brandes-style shortest-path accumulation.
e.brent-method>toms-748: TOMS 748 refines bracketing interpolation root finding of the same kind as Brent's method to achieve higher asymptotic efficiency.
e.bresenham-line>amanatides-woo: Its structure extends DDA-style line traversal, which visits grid cells incrementally in order, to 3D ray traversal
e.bresenham-line>bresenham-circle: The same author extends incremental integer rasterization to circular arcs
e.bresenham-line>xiaolin-wu-line: Adds pixel intensity distribution to the same incremental line rasterization
e.brief>orb: The ORB paper states that it steers the BRIEF descriptor by keypoint orientation and selects its bit tests by learning
e.brodal-queue>strict-fibonacci-heap: Brodal et al. achieved, with a simpler structure on a pointer machine, the worst-case bounds that the Brodal queue had obtained on the RAM model.
e.bron-kerbosch>clique-percolation: It needs a step that finds the cliques of the graph before building communities.
e.bron-kerbosch>tomita-pivot: The paper adds pivot selection to a depth-first search that prunes as in Bron–Kerbosch and proves a worst-case time bound.
e.brzozowski-derivatives>antimirov-deriv: As its title says, generalizes derivatives of regular expressions to partial derivatives split into sets of expressions.
e.bst>avl-tree: The first self-balancing tree, adding a height-balance condition to the binary search tree (Knuth TAOCP Vol.3 §6.2.3)
e.bst>cartesian-tree: The Cartesian tree satisfies binary-search-tree order on positions and heap order on values at the same time.
e.bst>kd-tree: As the paper's title says, generalizes binary search trees to multiple dimensions
e.bst>quadtree: The quadtree generalizes the binary search tree to two dimensions, each node branching four ways.
e.bst>randomized-bst: The paper adds randomized root insertion to an ordinary binary search tree to maintain the random-tree distribution.
e.bst>range-tree: The range tree is a multilevel structure that nests balanced binary search trees, one level per coordinate.
e.bst>rope-string: A rope represents a string as a binary tree whose leaves are string pieces.
e.bst>scapegoat-tree: The scapegoat tree keeps a plain binary search tree, with no extra node data, balanced by partial rebuilding.
e.bst>skip-list: Presented as an alternative to balanced trees, but not derived from trees
e.bst>splay-tree: Defined as a binary search tree that self-adjusts via rotations
e.bst>treap: By definition, keys satisfy binary search tree order (the name is tree + heap)
e.bst>weight-balanced-tree: The weight-balanced tree is a binary search tree whose balance is defined by subtree size ratios.
e.bubble-sort>comb-sort: Dobosiewicz's paper presents the method, in its very title, as an efficient variation of bubble sort.
e.buffer-tree>b-epsilon-tree: Like the buffer tree, the Bε-tree collects updates in internal-node buffers and pushes them down in batches.
e.bulk-synchronous-parallel>pregel: The Pregel paper applies superstep-based computation inspired by Valiant's BSP model to graph processing
e.bvh>slab-method: Kay and Kajiya used bounding volumes built from pairs of parallel planes (slabs) in the hierarchy and tested them by ray–slab intersection
e.bvh>surface-area-heuristic: Goldsmith and Salmon introduced surface-area-based cost estimation for the automatic construction of bounding volume hierarchies
e.bwt>bwa: As its title says, aligns short reads using the Burrows–Wheeler transform.
e.bwt>bzip2: Uses the Burrows–Wheeler transform as the block-sorting stage
e.bwt>fm-index: Compressed index that adds rank-query structures on top of the BWT
e.byzantine-agreement>pbft: PBFT was presented as a replication protocol that solves the Byzantine generals (Byzantine agreement) problem practically in asynchronous networks
e.calic>loco-i: Both are contemporary lossless image compression methods based on context-based prediction and residual coding
e.camshift>mean-shift-tracking: Both are tracking methods that locate the target from its color distribution using mean-shift iterations
e.canonical-huffman>deflate: DEFLATE defines its Huffman codes in canonical form so that they can be rebuilt from code lengths alone
e.cart>gradient-boosting: Uses regression trees as weak learners
e.cart>id3: Decision tree induction methods developed independently around the same time
e.cartesian-tree>bender-farach-colton-lc: The paper uses the Cartesian tree to reduce general RMQ to the LCA problem.
e.cartesian-tree>fischer-heun-rmq: The Fischer–Heun method classifies blocks by Cartesian-tree shape so that they can share tables.
e.cartesian-tree>treap: The treap is defined as a Cartesian tree with random priorities and cites Vuillemin's Cartesian trees.
e.catmull-clark>loop-subdivision: Applies weighted-averaging rules of the same kind as approximating subdivision for quad meshes to triangle meshes
e.cbc-mode>ccm: Uses CBC-MAC, computed by CBC chaining, for the authentication part
e.cbc-mode>cmac: As its title says, a one-key variant of CBC-MAC, which computes a MAC by CBC chaining
e.ccd-ik>fabrik: Solves the same iterative inverse kinematics problem by repositioning joints instead of rotating them
e.celt>opus: RFC 6716 defines Opus as a codec combining a SILK layer and a CELT layer
e.cfrac>quadratic-sieve: The quadratic sieve keeps the factor-base and congruence-of-squares framework of continued fraction factorization but finds smooth values by sieving instead of trial division
e.chacha20-poly1305>wireguard: The paper states that the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD is used to encrypt data
e.chacha>blake: The BLAKE proposal states that its compression function core uses a modified ChaCha
e.chacha>chacha20-poly1305: RFC 7539 defines the AEAD combination of ChaCha20 and Poly1305
e.chaikin>doo-sabin: Its structure extends corner-cutting curve subdivision to quadratic B-spline surface subdivision
e.chaitin-register-allocation>iterated-r: Iterated register coalescing improves Chaitin-style graph-coloring allocation by interleaving coalescing.
e.chaitin-register-allocation>linear-sca: Linear scan was presented as a faster alternative to graph-coloring allocation.
e.chang-roberts>bully-algorithm: Both are distributed leader-election algorithms that elect the process with the largest identifier
e.chd>bbhash: Addresses the same problem of building minimal perfect hash functions, but BBHash uses cascading bit arrays.
e.chd>recsplit: Addresses the same problem of building minimal perfect hash functions, but RecSplit uses recursive splitting and exhaustive search.
e.cheney>baker-gc: Baker extended Cheney's copying collection algorithm into a real-time version performed incrementally, interleaved with program execution
e.cheney>generational-gc: Ungar's generation scavenging uses copying collection for the young generation
e.chew-second-algorithm>ruppert-refineme: Both are Delaunay-refinement methods for quality mesh generation published around the same time, sharing the framework of inserting circumcenters of bad triangles and splitting boundaries.
e.classical-mds>isomap: Isomap applies classical MDS to the matrix of geodesic distances.
e.clauset-newman-moore>louvain: The Louvain paper compares against CNM greedy modularity optimization and presents a faster multilevel method.
e.clinger-algorithm>eisel-lemire: Lemire's paper presents a method that also converts most inputs outside Clinger's fast path exactly with 64-bit integer multiplications
e.cmac>eax: EAX uses OMAC to authenticate the nonce, header and ciphertext
e.cmac>siv: AES-SIV computes the synthetic IV with a CMAC-based PRF
e.conjugate-gradient>bicgstab: As its title states, it is presented as a variant of Bi-CG, the nonsymmetric extension of the conjugate gradient method.
e.conjugate-gradient>lobpcg: As its title states, it is a locally optimal block form of the preconditioned conjugate gradient method for eigenvalue computation.
e.conjugate-gradient>lsqr: The LSQR paper states that the method is analytically equivalent to the conjugate gradient method.
e.conjugate-gradient>nonlinear-conjugate: The Fletcher–Reeves paper extends the conjugate gradient method to minimizing general, non-quadratic functions.
e.conjugate-gradient>powell-method: Powell's method applies the concept of conjugate directions to derivative-free search.
e.connected-component-labeling>suzuki-ab: Both deal with connected components of binary images; the Suzuki–Abe method traces their borders and hierarchy
e.consistent-hashing>chord: States that it uses consistent hashing to assign nodes and keys
e.consistent-hashing>jump-consistent-has: Presented as achieving the same properties as consistent hashing without storage
e.consistent-hashing>rendezvous-hashing: Solves the same distributed assignment problem in a different way
e.constrained-delaunay>chew-second-algor: Chew's second algorithm is a refinement scheme that repeatedly inserts circumcenters into a constrained Delaunay triangulation.
e.constrained-delaunay>sweep-line-cdt: The paper states in its title and text that it presents a sweep-line algorithm for constructing the constrained Delaunay triangulation.
e.contrastive-divergence>deep-belief-net: The greedy layer-wise training of deep belief nets trains each RBM with contrastive divergence
e.cook-torrance>schlick-fresnel: Approximates the Fresnel term of microfacet BRDFs with an inexpensive polynomial
e.copying-gc>cheney: Presents a way to perform copying GC without recursion
e.copying-gc>immix: Immix also uses copying collection, opportunistically evacuating live objects out of fragmented blocks
e.count-sketch>count-min-sketch: Both estimate frequencies from hashed counter arrays; Count–Min drops the sign hash and takes the minimum.
e.counting-bloom-filter>tinylfu: TinyLFU estimates access frequencies compactly with an approximate counting structure from the counting Bloom filter family
e.counting-sort>radix-sort: LSD radix sort applies a stable counting sort to each digit (CLRS §8.3)
e.crc>crc32c: Castagnoli et al. searched for and proposed 32-bit generator polynomials that improve the detection performance of CRCs.
e.crc>table-driven-crc: Sarwate's paper presents a way to speed up CRC computation with table lookups.
e.criminisi-inpainting>patchmatch: Both are used for image completion that fills missing regions with similar patches found elsewhere in the image
e.crossing-number-pip>hormann-agathos-pi: The paper shows that the ray-crossing method of the even–odd rule is closely related to the winding number and derives from this an algorithm computing the winding number for arbitrary polygons.
e.ctr-mode>ccm: CCM is defined as the combination of counter-mode encryption and CBC-MAC authentication
e.ctr-mode>eax: EAX is presented as a combination of counter-mode encryption and OMAC authentication
e.ctr-mode>gcm: As the name says, combines counter-mode encryption with Galois-field authentication
e.ctr-mode>siv: Performs counter-mode encryption starting from the synthetic IV
e.cubic>hystart: HyStart was designed by the same group for use with CUBIC and is implemented inside the Linux CUBIC module.
e.cuckoo-hashing>cuckoo-filter: The paper describes storing fingerprints with partial-key cuckoo hashing
e.cuckoo-hashing>hopscotch-hashing: The paper's abstract says the hopscotch technique has the flavors of chaining, cuckoo hashing and linear probing; cuckoo hashing is one of them.
e.cycle-canceling>min-mean-cycle-canceli: The paper shows that, in the classical method of repeatedly canceling negative cycles, a judicious choice of cycles bounds the number of iterations polynomially.
e.cyk>earley: Solves the same general context-free parsing problem with a chart-based approach
e.cyrus-beck>liang-barsky: Computer graphics textbooks present both as parametric line clipping and describe Liang–Barsky as an independently developed method that is especially fast for axis-aligned regions.
e.cytron-ssa>braun-ssa: Braun et al. compare against the method of Cytron et al. and offer an alternative that needs no dominance-frontier computation.
e.d-star>d-star-lite: The paper states that D* Lite implements the same navigation strategy as D*.
e.dbscan>hdbscan: The HDBSCAN paper generalizes DBSCAN into a cluster hierarchy over all density thresholds.
e.dbscan>optics: The OPTICS paper extends DBSCAN's density-based cluster notion to an ordering of points that covers many density levels.
e.dct>clenshaw-curtis: The Chebyshev coefficients and weights of Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature can be computed with the discrete cosine transform.
e.ddpg>sac: SAC is, like DDPG, an off-policy actor-critic with a replay buffer, and the paper compares it directly with DDPG.
e.ddpg>td3: The TD3 paper reduces DDPG's overestimation and variance problems with three modifications.
e.ddpm>classifier-free-guidance: Classifier-free guidance is defined by combining the conditional and unconditional noise predictions of a diffusion model
e.ddpm>ddim: DDIM generalizes the Markovian forward process of DDPM to non-Markovian processes with the same objective
e.ddpm>latent-diffusion: Latent diffusion moves the training of pixel-space diffusion models into the latent space of an autoencoder
e.deep-belief-network>denoising-autoenco: The denoising autoencoder was proposed as an alternative to RBMs for layer-wise pretraining of deep networks
e.deepwalk>node2vec: The node2vec paper presents a generalization that reduces to DeepWalk's uniform random walks when p = q = 1.
e.deflate>zopfli: The Zopfli announcement describes it as a compressor that produces smaller DEFLATE-compatible output
e.dekker-algorithm>dijkstra-mutex: Dijkstra's 1965 solution generalizes the mutual exclusion handled by Dekker's two-process solution to N processes
e.dekker-algorithm>peterson-algorithm: Peterson's paper presents a two-process mutual exclusion solution that is simpler than Dekker's algorithm
e.des>serpent: The FSE 1998 proposal states that it uses the DES S-boxes in a new structure
e.dfp>bfgs: Fletcher's 1970 paper treats a family of variable metric updates that includes the DFP formula and presents the BFGS update.
e.dfs>chain-decomposition: The chain decomposition is defined from a depth-first search tree and its back edges.
e.dfs>dancing-links: Dancing links implements the choose-and-undo steps of a depth-first backtracking search for exact covers with linked-list operations.
e.dfs>gabow-scc: As its title says, the paper computes strong and biconnected components with path-based depth-first search.
e.dfs>hopcroft-tarjan-bcc: Algorithm 447 finds articulation points and biconnected components on top of depth-first search.
e.dfs>hopcroft-tarjan-planarity: The paper presents a linear-time planarity test that uses depth-first search.
e.dfs>ida-star: Each iteration is a depth-first search within the f-value bound
e.dfs>kosaraju-scc: Applies DFS twice, to the original graph and to its transpose (CLRS §22.5)
e.dfs>lengauer-tarjan: Semidominators are defined and computed from depth-first search numbers.
e.dfs>tarjan-scc: The paper's title and body state that it is based on depth-first search
e.dfs>tiernan-cycles: It is a backtracking search that extends paths depth-first.
e.dfs>topological-sort: DFS finishing order also yields a topological sort, but Kahn's method is based on in-degrees
e.dial>delta-stepping: It widens per-distance buckets into buckets of width Δ so that vertices in the same bucket can be processed in parallel.
e.diffie-hellman>double-ratchet: The specification defines the Diffie–Hellman ratchet as a core component
e.diffie-hellman>ecc: Miller proposed carrying Diffie–Hellman key exchange over to elliptic curve groups
e.diffie-hellman>eke: Includes a variant that exchanges ephemeral Diffie–Hellman values encrypted under the password
e.diffie-hellman>elgamal: Presented as public-key encryption and signatures based on the Diffie–Hellman key distribution scheme
e.diffie-hellman>noise-protocol: The specification defines handshakes as patterns of Diffie–Hellman operations
e.diffie-hellman>rsa: Realizes the public-key concept proposed by Diffie and Hellman under a different mathematical assumption
e.diffie-hellman>station-to-station: Adds authentication to the Diffie–Hellman exchange through signatures and encryption
e.diffie-hellman>x25519: As its title says, a fast Diffie–Hellman key exchange on a specific elliptic curve
e.diffie-hellman>x3dh: As its name (Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman) says, combines several Diffie–Hellman values
e.diffusion-model>ddpm: DDPM improves the diffusion probabilistic model of Sohl-Dickstein et al. with a noise-prediction parameterization
e.dijkstra-mutex>lamport-bakery: Lamport's paper presents the bakery algorithm, as its title says, as a new solution of Dijkstra's concurrent programming control problem
e.dijkstra>a-star: A* with heuristic h = 0 is identical to Dijkstra (Russell and Norvig, AIMA)
e.dijkstra>bidirectional-search: A variant that runs Dijkstra-style searches simultaneously from both the source and the target.
e.dijkstra>brandes-betweenness: On weighted graphs it counts shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm.
e.dijkstra>crp: Its customization and query phases use Dijkstra-style searches on the multilevel graph.
e.dijkstra>delta-stepping: With small Δ it approaches Dijkstra's approach of settling vertices in distance order.
e.dijkstra>dial: It is an implementation of Dijkstra's algorithm with the priority queue replaced by an array of distance buckets.
e.dijkstra>duan-sssp: It aims to improve on the O(m + n log n) time bound of Dijkstra's algorithm on sparse graphs.
e.dijkstra>eppstein-k-shortest-paths: It first computes a shortest-path tree and then builds the path graph from sidetrack edges.
e.dijkstra>johnson: Runs Dijkstra from each vertex after reweighting
e.dijkstra>jonker-volgenant: It finds shortest augmenting paths with a Dijkstra-like search over reduced costs.
e.dijkstra>link-state-routing: In the new ARPANET routing algorithm each node runs a shortest-path-first (Dijkstra) computation over the whole topology.
e.dijkstra>radix-heap: The radix heap was designed as the priority queue for Dijkstra's algorithm.
e.dijkstra>ramalingam-reps: It reprocesses only the vertices affected by a change, using a priority queue in a Dijkstra-like manner.
e.dijkstra>suurballe: It performs two shortest-path computations, the second on a graph reweighted with reduced costs.
e.dijkstra>thorup-sssp: It avoids the sorting bottleneck by ordering visits with an MST-based hierarchy instead of Dijkstra's distance order.
e.dijkstra>yen-k-shortest-paths: It repeatedly calls a shortest-path algorithm as a subroutine to compute the remaining path at each spur vertex.
e.dinic>edmonds-karp: Improvements based on shortest augmenting paths, published independently of each other
e.dinic>hopcroft-karp: Its phase structure of finding a blocking flow in a layered graph matches Dinic's algorithm, of which it can be viewed as a bipartite-matching specialization.
e.distance-transform>felzenszwalb-distan: The paper states that the distance transform of sampled functions generalizes the classical distance transform of binary images
e.distributed-ray-tracing>path-tracing: Path tracing generalizes the stochastic sampling of distributed ray tracing into a Monte Carlo solution of the rendering equation
e.divide-and-conquer-delaunay>guibas-sto: The Guibas–Stolfi algorithm implements Delaunay triangulation with the same divide-and-merge structure in a simpler way using the quad-edge data structure and two geometric predicates.
e.divide-and-conquer-voronoi>alpha-shape: The alpha-shape paper computes the α-hull and α-shape from the Voronoi diagram of the point set in O(n log n) time.
e.divide-and-conquer-voronoi>divide-and-: The Delaunay triangulation is the dual of the Voronoi diagram, and the divide-and-conquer Delaunay algorithm carries out the same split-and-merge structure as the divide-and-conquer Voronoi construction on the dual side.
e.divide-and-conquer-voronoi>fortune: Both construct the planar Voronoi diagram in O(n log n); Fortune's algorithm uses a plane sweep instead of divide and conquer.
e.dixon-factorization>quadratic-sieve: The quadratic sieve uses the same congruence-of-squares principle as Dixon's method but collects smooth relations quickly by sieving values of x²−n
e.dot-product-attention>transformer: States that it is identical to dot-product attention except for the scaling factor
e.double-q-learning>double-dqn: The paper carries the idea of Double Q-learning over to DQN to reduce overestimation.
e.double-q-learning>td3: TD3 uses the minimum of two critics (clipped double Q), an idea drawn from Double Q-learning.
e.douglas-rachford>admm: ADMM is known to be equivalent to Douglas–Rachford splitting applied to the dual problem.
e.dqn>ddpg: The DDPG paper carries the ingredients behind DQN's success (replay buffer, target networks) over to continuous action spaces.
e.dqn>double-dqn: Double DQN is a variant of DQN that changes only how the target value is computed.
e.dqn>dueling-dqn: The dueling architecture replaces the Q-network of DQN-style algorithms with separate value and advantage streams.
e.dqn>prioritized-experience-replay: The paper improves DQN by replacing its uniform experience replay with prioritized sampling based on temporal-difference error.
e.dragon4>grisu: Loitsch's paper presents Grisu, which prints quickly using only fixed-width integers instead of the big-integer arithmetic of Steele and White's method
e.dropout>alexnet: States that dropout is used in the fully connected layers
e.dropout>gelu: The GELU paper derives GELU from a stochastic regularizer combining properties of dropout, zoneout and ReLUs
e.dropout>transformer: States that dropout is applied to the output of each sub-layer
e.dsa>ecdsa: Signature scheme that carries DSA over to elliptic curve groups
e.dutch-national-flag>american-flag-sort: By analogy with the three-way Dutch national flag problem, the paper calls the general many-way problem the American flag problem.
e.dutch-national-flag>bentley-mcilroy-pa: It solves the same three-way partitioning problem by gathering equal keys at both ends and moving them afterwards.
e.ear-clipping>fist: FIST is a practical implementation of repeated ear clipping augmented with geometric hashing and robustness measures.
e.ecc>bls-signature: Represents a signature as a single curve point using a pairing on elliptic curves
e.ecc>eddsa: Uses twisted Edwards curve group operations
e.ecc>x25519: Elliptic-curve cryptography defined on a Montgomery-form curve
e.ecn>dctcp: DCTCP uses the fraction of ECN marks set by switches as its congestion signal.
e.edmonds-blossom>blossom-v: As its title states, it is a new implementation of the blossom-based minimum-cost perfect matching algorithm.
e.edmonds-blossom>chinese-postman: As its title indicates, the paper solves the Chinese postman problem by combining matching with Euler tours.
e.edmonds-blossom>christofides: Its step that computes a minimum-cost perfect matching on odd-degree vertices requires a general-graph matching algorithm.
e.edmonds-blossom>chu-liu-edmonds: Its technique of contracting a cycle into a single vertex and expanding it later has the same structure as blossom shrinking.
e.eight-point-algorithm>five-point-algor: Both recover the relative pose (essential matrix) of two views from correspondences; the five-point solver uses the minimal number of correspondences
e.eke>spake2: As its title says, presented as a simplified variant of the EKE family
e.eke>srp: Develops EKE-style password-authenticated key exchange so that the server stores only a verifier
e.elgamal>cramer-shoup: Adds validity-check values to an ElGamal-style ciphertext
e.elgamal>dsa: Described as a variant of ElGamal signatures (Menezes et al., Handbook of Applied Cryptography §11.5)
e.elgamal>schnorr-signature: A later scheme in the discrete-log signature family, but no explicit statement of direct derivation found
e.elias-gamma>elias-delta: In the same paper, the delta code is defined to encode the length of the integer with the gamma code
e.elias-gamma>fibonacci-coding: Both are universal codes for positive integers with no known upper bound
e.elman-network>bidirectional-rnn: The bidirectional RNN extends the regular one-directional recurrent network with separate forward and backward hidden layers
e.elman-network>lstm: The LSTM paper compares against earlier recurrent networks such as Elman nets, which fail on long-term dependencies
e.em>coherent-point-drift: The paper formulates registration as probability density estimation with a Gaussian mixture model and optimizes it with the EM algorithm.
e.em>latent-dirichlet-allocation: The LDA paper estimates the model parameters with variational EM.
e.em>plsa: pLSA is trained with the (tempered) EM algorithm.
e.environment-mapping>cube-mapping: Greene presented storing environment maps as projections onto the six faces of a cube
e.environment-mapping>sh-irradiance: Represents irradiance environment maps for diffuse lighting with nine spherical harmonic coefficients
e.epidemic-gossip>swim: SWIM states in its title and text that membership changes are disseminated by infection-style (epidemic) gossip
e.euclidean-algorithm>binary-gcd: A structural variant that computes the same GCD as the Euclidean algorithm using only shifts and subtraction instead of division
e.euclidean-algorithm>lehmer-gcd: Lehmer's paper, as its title says, presents a way to accelerate Euclid's algorithm for large numbers
e.ewa-splatting>gaussian-splatting: Follows the EWA splatting approach of Zwicker et al. to project 3D Gaussians onto the screen
e.extended-kalman-filter>unscented-kalma: The UKF is presented as an alternative that reduces the Jacobian linearization errors of the extended Kalman filter
e.extendible-hashing>linear-hashing: Both are dynamic hashing schemes that split buckets as the file grows; linear hashing splits in a fixed order without a directory.
e.ezw>ebcot: Both code wavelet coefficients in bit-plane order to produce an embedded bitstream
e.ezw>spiht: The SPIHT paper develops the zerotree principle of EZW into set partitioning in hierarchical trees
e.fair-queuing>deficit-round-robin: The DRR paper aims to approximate fair queueing with O(1) work per packet.
e.fair-queuing>stochastic-fair-queuing: SFQ approximates fair queueing probabilistically and cheaply by hashing flows onto a fixed set of queues.
e.fair-queuing>weighted-fair-queuing: Parekh and Gallager note that PGPS is the weighted fair queueing of Demers et al. and analyze it as a generalization through GPS.
e.fast-corner>orb: The ORB paper states that it combines an oriented FAST detector with a rotation-aware BRIEF descriptor
e.fast-rcnn>faster-rcnn: Faster R-CNN combines the Fast R-CNN detector with an RPN that generates the proposals
e.fasta>blast: The BLAST paper cites FASTP and FASTA as earlier word-hit heuristics, and Lipman co-authored both methods.
e.faster-rcnn>mask-rcnn: Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN by adding a mask prediction branch
e.fcn>mask-rcnn: The mask branch of Mask R-CNN is a small FCN applied to each region of interest
e.fcn>u-net: U-Net builds on the fully convolutional network and enlarges its expanding path
e.feldman-vss>pedersen-commitment: Introduces the commitment while improving Feldman's VSS to be information-theoretically hiding
e.fft>bluestein-fft: Computes arbitrary-length DFTs via convolutions using power-of-two FFTs
e.fft>dct: The original DCT paper also shows how to compute the transform using the FFT.
e.fft>goertzel: Both compute the DFT, but the Goertzel algorithm evaluates individual frequency components recursively instead of the full transform.
e.fft>good-thomas-fft: Both decompose the DFT into smaller DFTs, but Good–Thomas uses the Chinese remainder theorem without twiddle factors.
e.fft>rader-fft: Computes prime-length DFTs via FFT-based cyclic convolution
e.fft>schonhage-strassen: Computes the convolution with a number-theoretic FFT
e.fft>split-radix-fft: The split-radix FFT is a variant of the Cooley–Tukey FFT that mixes radix-2 and radix-4 decompositions.
e.fiat-shamir>ml-dsa: Turns an identification scheme into a signature with Lyubashevsky's 'Fiat–Shamir with aborts' technique
e.fiat-shamir>schnorr-signature: Schnorr turned his identification scheme into a signature using the Fiat–Shamir approach
e.fibonacci-heap>brodal-queue: The Brodal queue attains the amortized time bounds of Fibonacci heaps in the worst case.
e.fibonacci-heap>hollow-heap: The hollow heap paper obtains the same amortized bounds as Fibonacci heaps by using lazy deletion.
e.fibonacci-heap>rank-pairing-heap: The paper shows that rank-pairing heaps match the amortized bounds of Fibonacci heaps without cascading cuts.
e.fibonacci-heap>strict-fibonacci-heap: The strict Fibonacci heap turns the amortized bounds of Fibonacci heaps into worst-case bounds on a pointer machine.
e.fks-perfect-hashing>chd: Shares the two-level structure of splitting keys into buckets first and then finding a collision-free placement for each bucket.
e.flajolet-martin>loglog: Follow-up work by the same author (Flajolet) that changes the observable to reduce memory
e.flash-attention>flash-attention-2: Successor that improves FlashAttention's work partitioning
e.fletcher-checksum>adler-32: RFC 1950 describes Adler-32 as a 32-bit extension and improvement of the Fletcher algorithm.
e.floyd-steinberg>jarvis-judice-ninke: Both are error-diffusion methods that spread quantization error to neighbors; JJN uses a wider diffusion kernel
e.floyd-warshall>isomap: Isomap approximates geodesic distances by all-pairs shortest paths in the neighborhood graph.
e.fm-index>bowtie: States that it indexes the reference genome with a scheme based on the Burrows–Wheeler transform and the FM-index.
e.fm-index>bwa: Uses the occurrence queries of the FM-index for backward search on the BWT.
e.ford-fulkerson>boykov-kolmogorov: It is an augmenting-path maximum-flow algorithm that reuses its search trees instead of rebuilding them in each iteration.
e.ford-fulkerson>dinic: Batches the augmenting-path method using level graphs and blocking flows
e.ford-fulkerson>edmonds-karp: Improvement of Ford–Fulkerson that chooses shortest paths as augmenting paths
e.ford-fulkerson>gomory-hu-tree: It constructs the tree by repeating maximum-flow/minimum-cut computations n−1 times.
e.ford-fulkerson>graph-cut-segmentation: Graph-cut segmentation obtains the minimum cut with a max-flow algorithm, following the max-flow min-cut theorem
e.ford-fulkerson>push-relabel: A different approach to the same maximum-flow problem, using preflows and distance labels instead of augmenting paths.
e.frame-of-reference>pfordelta: PFOR (patched frame of reference) was presented as frame-of-reference coding extended with exception handling
e.funk-svd>bpr: The BPR paper shows how to train matrix factorization models with a pairwise ranking criterion.
e.funk-svd>implicit-als: Implicit-feedback ALS fits latent-factor matrix factorization to a confidence-weighted preference matrix and solves it by alternating least squares.
e.funk-svd>svd-plus-plus: SVD++ adds an implicit-feedback term to the latent-factor matrix factorization used in the Netflix Prize.
e.furer>harvey-van-der-hoeven: Cites the line of improvements following Fürer and reaches O(n log n)
e.gae>ppo: The algorithm in the PPO paper uses GAE for advantage estimation.
e.gale-shapley>stable-roommates: It handles the extension of the bipartite stable marriage problem to a single set, and its first-phase proposal process resembles Gale–Shapley.
e.galil-rule>apostolico-giancarlo: Galil's strategy is named in the paper's title, which revisits it to present a new variant.
e.gauss-seidel>multigrid: Multigrid uses Gauss–Seidel-type relaxation sweeps as the smoothing step on each grid level.
e.gauss-seidel>sor: Young's paper accelerates Gauss–Seidel (Liebmann) iteration by introducing an overrelaxation factor.
e.gcm>gcm-siv: As its title says, a variant that reorganizes GCM's components in the SIV style
e.gcn>gat: GAT replaces the fixed neighbor weights of GCN with learned attention coefficients
e.gcn>graphsage: GraphSAGE generalizes the transductive GCN approach to an inductive one that applies to unseen nodes
e.generational-gc>g1-gc: The G1 paper describes G1 as a region-based collector with a generational mode that collects young regions separately
e.gentry-fhe>bgv: As its title says, achieves leveled full homomorphism without Gentry-style bootstrapping
e.gentry-fhe>tfhe: Improves Gentry's bootstrapping so that it runs quickly after every gate
e.geohash>h3: Both systems address the same geospatial indexing problem of dividing the Earth's surface into hierarchical cells and assigning each cell a string or integer index.
e.gibbs-sampling>contrastive-divergence: The paper estimates the negative-phase statistics with a few steps of alternating Gibbs sampling started at the data
e.gibbs-sampling>slice-sampling: Slice sampling can be seen as a Gibbs-style update that alternately samples a height and a position from a joint distribution augmented with an auxiliary height variable
e.gk-quantile-summary>kll-sketch: Solves the same streaming quantile approximation problem with randomized compactors.
e.gk-quantile-summary>t-digest: Solves the same streaming quantile estimation problem with centroid clusters.
e.glu>swiglu: The paper compares GLU variants that replace the sigmoid with other functions, including SwiGLU
e.glushkov-construction>thompson-constru: Both construct an NFA proportional in size to a regular expression, but there is no evidence of derivation.
e.golomb-coding>exp-golomb: Its structure replaces the fixed-size intervals of the Golomb code with exponentially growing ones
e.golomb-coding>loco-i: LOCO-I codes prediction residuals with Golomb-type codes whose parameters are chosen per context
e.golomb-coding>rice-coding: The Rice code is equivalent to the special case of the Golomb code whose parameter is a power of two
e.golub-kahan-bidiagonalization>golub-re: The Golub–Reinsch algorithm first bidiagonalizes the matrix in the Golub–Kahan manner and then computes the singular values.
e.golub-kahan-bidiagonalization>lsqr: The LSQR paper states that the method is based on the Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization procedure.
e.gomory-hu-tree>gusfield: The paper presents simpler methods that compute Gomory–Hu trees without node contractions.
e.good-thomas-fft>winograd-fft: Winograd's algorithm combines short DFT modules through Good–Thomas-style prime-factor index mapping.
e.googlenet>mobilenet: The MobileNet paper notes that Inception models used depthwise separable convolutions to reduce computation
e.googlenet>yolo: The YOLO paper states that its network architecture is inspired by the GoogLeNet classification model
e.gotoh>myers-miller: Combines Gotoh's affine-gap alignment recurrences with a computation in linear space.
e.gotoh>wavefront-alignment: Reformulates and computes the Gotoh-style gap-affine alignment recurrences in terms of wavefronts.
e.gouraud-shading>phong-shading: Phong interpolates normals instead of vertex intensities, fixing the loss of highlights in Gouraud shading
e.grace-hash-join>hybrid-hash-join: The hybrid hash join combines the partitioning of the GRACE hash join with joining the first partition directly in memory
e.gradient-boosting>catboost: CatBoost is a variant of gradient boosting that reduces its prediction shift through ordered boosting and categorical-feature handling.
e.gradient-boosting>lightgbm: Improves GBDT training efficiency with GOSS and EFB
e.gradient-boosting>xgboost: Presented as a scalable implementation of gradient tree boosting
e.gradient-descent>armijo-line-search: Armijo's paper proposes a step-size rule for steepest descent and proves its convergence.
e.gradient-descent>levenberg-marquardt: Marquardt's paper presents an algorithm that interpolates between the Gauss–Newton (Taylor series) method and gradient descent.
e.gradient-descent>madgwick-filter: Madgwick's paper, as its title says, corrects the orientation error with a gradient-descent algorithm and fuses it with gyroscope integration
e.gradient-descent>momentum: Proposes adding an inertia term to gradient methods to accelerate convergence
e.gradient-descent>sgd: Gradient descent with the full gradient replaced by a stochastic estimate (Robbins–Monro stochastic approximation is the theoretical basis)
e.graham-scan>akl-toussaint: The Akl–Toussaint heuristic is a preprocessing step that discards interior points and is placed in front of sorting-based hull algorithms such as Graham scan.
e.graham-scan>chan-hull: Combines per-group Graham scans with a Jarvis march
e.graham-scan>melkman: Both maintain hull vertices by pushing and popping with left-turn tests; Melkman's algorithm uses a deque operated at both ends instead of a stack.
e.graham-scan>monotone-chain: Described as a Graham scan variant that sorts by x-coordinate instead of polar angle
e.gram-schmidt>arnoldi-iteration: The Arnoldi process builds its basis by orthogonalizing Krylov vectors in the Gram–Schmidt manner.
e.graph-cut-segmentation>grabcut: The GrabCut paper describes extending Boykov–Jolly graph-cut segmentation with iterative estimation and Gaussian mixture color models
e.grisu>ryu: The Ryū paper compares against Grisu3 and presents a faster method that guarantees the shortest output for every input
e.guibas-stolfi-delaunay>dwyer-delaunay: Dwyer's algorithm keeps the Guibas–Stolfi divide-and-conquer framework but changes the partitioning to reduce the expected running time on uniformly distributed input.
e.halton-sequence>sobol-sequence: Both are multidimensional low-discrepancy sequences for quasi-Monte Carlo integration; no derivation is stated
e.hamming-code>bch-code: The single-error-correcting binary BCH code coincides with the Hamming code, so BCH codes are described as a multiple-error generalization of Hamming codes.
e.hamming-distance>levenshtein-distance: Widens the substitution-only Hamming distance to also allow insertions and deletions; both arose from error-correcting code research.
e.hamt>champ: The CHAMP paper changes the node layout of HAMTs to improve iteration speed and memory use.
e.hamt>ctrie: The Ctrie builds on the HAMT node structure to support lock-free concurrent updates.
e.hardware-transactional-memory>software: Shavit and Touitou proposed providing Herlihy and Moss's hardware transactional memory purely in software
e.harel-tarjan-lca>schieber-vishkin-lca: As their title says, Schieber and Vishkin simplified and parallelized the Harel–Tarjan LCA method.
e.harris-corner>shi-tomasi: References describe the Shi–Tomasi detector as a variant that uses the smaller eigenvalue of the structure tensor instead of the Harris response
e.hash-chaining>hopscotch-hashing: The paper's abstract says the hopscotch technique has the flavors of chaining, cuckoo hashing and linear probing; chaining is one of them.
e.hash-chaining>linear-probing: Same hash table with collision resolution switched from chaining to open addressing (Knuth TAOCP Vol.3 §6.4)
e.hash-chaining>timing-wheel: The hashed timing wheel hashes expiry times into the linked lists of a circular array's slots.
e.hash-chaining>two-choice-hashing: It is analyzed as a variant of chained hashing in which each key goes into the shorter of two candidate chains.
e.hazard-pointers>epoch-based-reclamatio: Both are memory-reclamation techniques for safely freeing removed nodes in lock-free data structures
e.heapsort>introsort: Ranges that exceed the recursion depth limit are handled by heapsort
e.heapsort>smoothsort: Dijkstra states that smoothsort is an in-situ sort inspired by heapsort.
e.heavy-path-decomposition>harel-tarjan-: The Harel–Tarjan LCA structure also uses the same heavy path decomposition, introduced independently.
e.hierholzer>chinese-postman: After duplicating paths so that all degrees become even, it uses a step that finds an Eulerian circuit.
e.hierholzer>christofides: It includes a step that finds an Eulerian circuit in the multigraph obtained after adding the matching.
e.hight>lea: A block cipher built only from ARX operations by the same Korean research group after HIGHT
e.highway-hierarchies>contraction-hierar: It is a follow-up from the same research group that simplifies hierarchical routing to rely solely on node contraction.
e.highway-network>resnet: The ResNet paper discusses highway networks, which use gated shortcuts, as concurrent related work
e.hilbert-curve>z-order-curve: Both are space-filling orders that give multidimensional points a one-dimensional order by recursively dividing the square into four cells.
e.hirschberg>myers-diff: Its linear-space refinement, which finds a middle point and recurses on both sides, has the same structure as Hirschberg's divide and conquer.
e.hirschberg>myers-miller: Applies Hirschberg's linear-space divide-and-conquer technique to affine-gap alignment.
e.hits>salsa: SALSA combines the hub and authority notions of HITS with the theory of random walks.
e.hkdf>double-ratchet: The specification recommends HKDF as the KDF for the root-key chain
e.hkdf>hpke: RFC 9180 defines and uses HKDF as its key derivation function
e.hkdf>tls-1-3-handshake: The RFC 8446 key schedule is defined with HKDF-Extract and HKDF-Expand
e.hmac>hkdf: Both the extract and expand steps of HKDF are built from HMAC
e.hmac>hotp: RFC 4226 defines HOTP as an HMAC-SHA-1 value over a counter
e.hmac>pbkdf2: RFC 2898 specifies HMAC-SHA-1 as the underlying pseudorandom function
e.hmc>nuts: The NUTS paper presents an extension of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo that sets the path length automatically
e.hopcroft-tarjan-bcc>hopcroft-tarjan-tr: The same authors extended biconnected decomposition to triconnected decomposition along separation pairs.
e.hopcroft-tarjan-bcc>tarjan-bridges: Articulation points and bridges are the same kind of cut-structure problem, and both are solved in linear time by comparing spanning-tree numbers.
e.hopcroft-tarjan-planarity>boyer-myrvol: It solves the same planarity-testing problem in linear time, using edge addition instead of path addition.
e.hopfield-network>boltzmann-machine: The Boltzmann machine uses a Hopfield-style energy function but updates units stochastically and adds hidden units
e.horn-quaternion>icp: Besl and McKay's ICP computes the optimal rigid transformation of the correspondences at each iteration with a closed-form unit-quaternion solution.
e.horn-schunck>lucas-kanade: Both are optical flow estimation methods based on brightness constancy, published in 1981
e.horner-method>clenshaw-algorithm: The Clenshaw recurrence generalizes Horner's method from the monomial basis to bases satisfying a three-term recurrence.
e.horspool>raita: As its title says, a tuning of Boyer–Moore–Horspool search that adjusts the comparison order.
e.horspool>wu-manber: Its bad-character shift table indexed by block hashes is structurally a widening of the Horspool shift to many patterns.
e.hotp>totp: RFC 6238 defines TOTP as an extension of HOTP that uses a time-based counter
e.hough-transform>ransac: Both are used to find models such as lines in point sets contaminated by outliers
e.householder-qr>golub-kahan-bidiagonali: The Golub–Kahan paper bidiagonalizes the matrix by applying Householder transformations from both sides.
